platforms.title: Restless Legs at Night? Your Evening Snack Might Be Behind It
platforms.meta_description: Restless legs syndrome is tied to brain iron and dopamine — but caffeine, alcohol, and carbs at night can make it noticeably worse.
platforms.body_html:
If your legs start crawling and twitching the moment you lie down, and the only relief is moving them, this is a recognizable pattern doctors call restless legs syndrome (RLS). Research reviewed in the NIH's PMC archive links RLS to low iron availability in the brain, which is needed to make dopamine, the chemical that helps regulate movement signals. What you eat in the evening doesn't cause RLS on its own, but it can make a bad night noticeably worse.

Dark Chocolate, Alcohol, and Refined Carbs Are Working Against You at Night

Dark chocolate and cocoa products contain both caffeine and theobromine, a related stimulant — together they overstimulate the nervous system in the hours before bed, and caffeine also interferes with how well the body absorbs iron. Mayo Clinic and multiple sleep-medicine reviews list caffeine and alcohol as the two substances most consistently tied to worse RLS symptoms. A drink in the evening might feel relaxing at first, but it disrupts sleep architecture later in the night, which is exactly when RLS symptoms tend to intensify.

Refined carbohydrates — white bread, pastries, sugary snacks — cause a fast rise and fall in blood sugar that can overstimulate the nervous system in a similar way. None of these foods are forbidden for life; the pattern that matters most is what's eaten in the few hours directly before bed, when the nervous system is already winding down and more sensitive to stimulation.

Where Iron Fits — and Where It Doesn't

Iron deficiency is one of the best-established contributors to RLS, but it's worth being precise about it: NIH-indexed research notes that low serum ferritin has only been reported in 10 to 20 percent of adults with RLS, so it's a real factor for some people, not the explanation for everyone. If RLS is frequent, checking ferritin levels with a doctor is worth doing before self-treating with iron supplements, since taking iron without a documented deficiency doesn't help and can cause its own side effects.

What About Magnesium?

Magnesium supplements come up almost as often as iron in casual advice for restless legs, but the evidence behind magnesium specifically is much thinner. Most of the RLS research base points to iron and dopamine, not magnesium status, and there isn't strong clinical evidence that magnesium supplementation reliably improves RLS symptoms the way correcting a documented iron deficiency can. That doesn't make a magnesium-rich diet a bad idea in general — leafy greens and nuts are useful foods regardless — it just means magnesium shouldn't be the first thing reached for instead of getting iron checked, especially if the crawling sensation shows up most nights rather than occasionally.

Three Swaps Worth Trying Tonight

  • Swap dark chocolate for a handful of nuts. Nuts contain some iron and none of the caffeine-theobromine combination.
  • Finish any alcohol 3 to 4 hours before bed. That gap gives the nervous system time to settle before the disrupted sleep phase kicks in.
  • Swap late-night bread or sweets for a boiled egg or unsweetened soy milk. Both are steadier on blood sugar and contain more iron than refined carbs.

None of this means giving up chocolate or wine permanently — it means noticing what's eaten in the window right before bed on the nights the crawling feeling is worst, and testing whether moving it earlier or swapping it out changes anything over a week or two. This content is general health information, not a diagnosis — a doctor should confirm RLS and check iron status rather than guessing from symptoms alone.
